code.title: Checked vs unchecked exceptions

followUps:
Because checked exceptions spread through every method signature and rarely help the caller recover. A SQLException thrown deep in a repository forces each layer above to declare it or wrap it, even though almost none can fix a broken database.

Frameworks such as Spring translate such failures into unchecked exceptions and handle them in one central place. Result: shorter signatures, no empty catch blocks written just to silence the compiler, and easier evolution (adding a new checked exception to an interface breaks every implementer and caller).

Badly: standard functional interfaces such as Function and Runnable do not declare checked exceptions, so a lambda body cannot throw them directly.

Example: paths.forEach(p -> Files.readString(p)) will not compile because readString throws IOException. Options: catch inside the lambda and wrap, or write your own interface.

stream.map(p -> {
  try { return Files.readString(p); }
  catch (IOException e) { throw new UncheckedIOException(e); }
})

Yes. Exception is checked, because only RuntimeException and its subclasses (plus Error) are exempt from the compiler's handle-or-declare rule.

So throw new Exception("x") inside a method forces a throws Exception clause or a try/catch. That is one reason throws Exception on every method is considered a smell: it tells callers nothing about what can actually go wrong.

code.title: Exception hierarchy walked with getSuperclass

followUps:
Because Throwable includes Error, which signals that the JVM itself may be in a bad state, such as OutOfMemoryError or StackOverflowError. Your code usually cannot repair that, and continuing may corrupt data.

Catching it also hides ThreadDeath-like signals and linkage errors. The normal rule is to catch the narrowest type you can handle. The exceptions are a top-level boundary (thread run loop, request handler) that logs and then lets the thread end or rethrows.

ClassNotFoundException is a checked exception thrown when you ask for a class by name at runtime and it is missing; NoClassDefFoundError is an Error thrown when a class was present when compiled but cannot be loaded now.

Example: Class.forName("com.x.Driver") with the jar absent gives the first. A class that was on the classpath at compile time but whose jar is missing at runtime, or whose static initializer failed earlier, gives the second. Fix the first by correcting the name or classpath; fix the second by checking packaging and the earlier failure.

It occurs when a static initializer block or a static field initializer throws an unchecked exception while a class is being initialized for the first time.

class Config {
  static final int N = Integer.parseInt("abc"); // throws
}
new Config(); // ExceptionInInitializerError
new Config(); // NoClassDefFoundError afterwards

The original exception is the cause. The class is then marked unusable, so every later use throws NoClassDefFoundError. Read the first stack trace in the log, not the later ones.

code.title: Tricky finally cases

followUps:
The compiler copies the finally block's code to every exit path of the try and catch, plus a catch-all handler that runs the code and rethrows. There is no special "finally" instruction in modern bytecode.

So a finally block with 5 lines and 3 exits (normal end, a return, and the exception path) appears 3 times in the class file. Older compilers used jsr/ret subroutines, which were removed from javac after Java 6. You can see this with javap -c.

The new exception from finally replaces the one in flight, and the original is lost (it is not even attached as suppressed).

try { throw new A(); }
finally { throw new B(); }
// caller sees only B

That is exactly the masking problem try-with-resources was designed to fix. If cleanup can fail, either wrap the cleanup in its own try/catch inside finally, or use try-with-resources so the primary exception wins and the other becomes suppressed.

Because return (or throw) inside finally overrides whatever the try block was doing, including silently discarding an exception that was about to propagate.

Example: the try throws IOException, finally says return 0, and the caller gets 0 with no error at all. Such bugs are hard to find because nothing is logged. javac warns with -Xlint:finally, and tools like SonarQube and ErrorProne flag it.

code.title: try-with-resources order and suppressed exceptions

followUps:
AutoCloseable.close() may throw any Exception and is meant for any resource; Closeable (in java.io) extends it, throws only IOException, and promises that closing twice has no effect (idempotent).

Use AutoCloseable for your own non-IO resources such as a lock guard or a transaction scope. Both work in try-with-resources. If you implement AutoCloseable, prefer declaring a narrower throws clause (or none) so callers have less to catch.

A null resource is allowed: try-with-resources simply skips the close() call for it, so there is no NullPointerException.

Example: try (InputStream in = maybeNull()) { ... } runs the body and closes nothing if in is null. It is your body that will fail if it uses in without a check. This null tolerance helps with factory methods that return null when nothing is available.

Put the resources in a list and close them in a loop, because the resource list in the try (...) header is fixed at compile time.

List<AutoCloseable> opened = new ArrayList<>();
try {
  for (Path p : paths) opened.add(Files.newInputStream(p));
} finally {
  for (int i = opened.size()-1; i >= 0; i--) opened.get(i).close();
}

Better: write a small wrapper class that implements AutoCloseable, closes all items in reverse order, and collects failures with addSuppressed. Then use that one object in try-with-resources.

code.title: Custom exception hierarchy mapped to HTTP codes

followUps:
Usually unchecked, unless the caller is expected to handle it as a normal business outcome. A balance check failing is a real expected case, so some teams do pick checked here.

Decide by asking: can the immediate caller do something useful (offer a smaller amount, ask for a top-up)? If yes and the API is small, checked makes the contract explicit. If it just travels up to a global handler that returns HTTP 422, unchecked is simpler and avoids signature clutter. Either way, keep it consistent across the code base.

Group by what the caller does differently, not by method: one class per kind of failure and put the specifics in fields, such as an error code and the ids involved.

Example: instead of CreateOrderFailedException, CancelOrderFailedException and so on, use NotFoundException(entity, id) and ConflictException(reason). Ten methods can then share two or three types, and the handler needs only one branch per type.

Use one central handler that maps each exception type (or error code) to a status, so no controller repeats it. In Spring that is a @RestControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler methods.

Typical mapping: validation error to 400, not found to 404, conflict to 409, dependency timeout to 503, anything unknown to 500 with a generic message (never the stack trace). Return a stable body such as problem-details JSON with the error code, and log the failure once there.

code.title: Exception chaining keeps the root cause

followUps:
The cause is the failure that made this exception happen ("this because of that"); suppressed exceptions are secondary failures that happened while handling the main one and would otherwise be lost.

Example: the body of a try-with-resources throws A, then close() throws B. A is the primary exception and B is in A.getSuppressed(). B did not cause A. A cause is set through the constructor or initCause; suppressed ones are added with addSuppressed.

It means that many stack frames of that cause are identical to the frames already shown for the enclosing exception, so Java omits them to keep the trace short.

The omitted frames are the common tail (usually the entry points like main or the thread pool worker). Example: a cause with 20 frames whose last 12 match the wrapper's frames prints 8 lines then ... 12 more. Nothing is lost: look above in the trace for the same frames.

Both are wrapper exceptions that carry the real failure of an async task as their cause, so you must call getCause() to see the original.

Future.get() throws ExecutionException; CompletableFuture.join() throws CompletionException, and get() on a CompletableFuture throws ExecutionException. Inside exceptionally or handle the exception may itself already be wrapped in CompletionException, so unwrap before matching on type.

code.title: Anti-patterns: swallowing and losing the cause

followUps:
Catching Exception is acceptable at a boundary where you truly must not let anything escape, and where you handle it properly: a thread's run loop, a request handler, a message consumer, or main.

At such a place log with the full stack trace, return a safe error or retry later, and keep the process alive. Do not do it deep in business logic, where it hides bugs. Also let Error and InterruptedException through, or restore the interrupt flag.

Log at the boundary where the exception is finally handled, once, not at every layer it passes through.

If a service catches, logs and rethrows, and the controller and the global handler also log, one failure appears as 3 log entries and the on-call engineer cannot tell how many failures occurred. Lower layers should add context by wrapping with a cause and let the top handler write the single log line with the whole chain.

Use static analysis in the build so a review does not depend on memory. Tools such as SonarQube, ErrorProne, SpotBugs and PMD flag empty catch blocks, catching Throwable, printStackTrace, and return in finally.

Run them in CI and fail the build on new violations. Add unit tests that check the exception type and cause, a code-review checklist for the rest, and compiler flags like -Xlint:all. Rules the tools cannot see (where to log) go in team guidelines.

code.title: Restoring the interrupt flag

followUps:
shutdownNow() calls interrupt() on every worker thread and returns the list of tasks that never started. It does not kill anything by force.

A task blocked in sleep, wait or queue.take wakes with InterruptedException. A task doing pure CPU work in a loop only stops if it checks Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted(). So a well-behaved task must respond to interruption, or shutdownNow will not make it stop.

No, the rules are the same: interrupt() on a virtual thread sets its flag and wakes blocking calls with InterruptedException, and you should still propagate it or restore the flag.

What changes is cost, not meaning: blocking a virtual thread is cheap, so you may have 100,000 of them, and cancelling them by interruption (or by StructuredTaskScope shutting down siblings) is the normal way to stop work. Code that swallows interrupts is just as broken.

Thread.interrupted() is a static method that returns the current thread's flag and clears it; isInterrupted() is an instance method that only reads the flag.

t.interrupt();
t.isInterrupted(); // true
t.isInterrupted(); // true
Thread.interrupted(); // true, now cleared
Thread.interrupted(); // false

Use isInterrupted() for loop checks, and interrupted() only when you consume the signal on purpose.

code.title: java.io streams vs java.nio channels and buffers

followUps:
A Selector lets one thread watch many non-blocking channels (sockets) and ask which of them are ready to read, write or accept, instead of dedicating a blocked thread to each connection.

Example: a chat server with 10,000 connections uses one or a few threads that loop on selector.select() and handle only the ready keys. Memory and context-switch cost stay small. Netty and many databases use this design. For a few connections, plain blocking I/O is simpler.

A heap buffer lives in the Java heap and is managed by the garbage collector; a direct buffer lives in native memory outside the heap.

Direct buffers avoid an extra copy when the OS reads or writes (the kernel can use the memory directly), so they suit large, long-lived I/O buffers. They cost more to allocate and are freed only when the GC cleans their wrapper object. Heap buffers are cheap and fine for small or short-lived data. Measure before choosing direct.

Because File has weak error reporting and few features, and Path/Files (Java 7) replaced it.

Examples: file.delete() and mkdir() return only a boolean, so you never learn why it failed, while Files.delete(path) throws NoSuchFileException or DirectoryNotEmptyException. File also lacks symbolic-link handling, attributes, atomic move, and directory walking. Use file.toPath() to bridge old code.

code.title: Streaming a large log with a top-K heap

followUps:
Count each IP in a hash map while streaming, then keep the 10 largest counts with a min-heap of size 10.

Map<String,Integer> c = new HashMap<>();
for each line: c.merge(ip, 1, Integer::sum);
PriorityQueue<Entry> h = min-heap by count;
for (e : c.entrySet()) { h.add(e); if (h.size() > 10) h.poll(); }

Time is O(n + u log 10) for n lines and u unique IPs; memory is O(u). If u is too large for RAM (say 500 million IPs), use a count-min sketch or split IPs by hash into files and count each partition separately.

Cut the file into byte ranges, then move each boundary forward to the next newline so no line is split between two workers.

Example: 50 GB and 8 workers gives ranges of about 6.25 GB. Worker k starts at offset k*size: if k>0 it skips forward to just after the first newline, and it keeps reading until it passes its end offset to finish the last line it started. Each worker keeps its own counters, which you merge at the end, so no locking is needed.

Open the file, remember the current offset, and poll for new bytes, reading only the lines appended since last time; or use a WatchService to get notified of changes.

Keep the position in a RandomAccessFile or channel, sleep briefly when you reach the end, and detect rotation by watching whether the file size shrinks or the file identity changes, then reopen. Only emit complete lines: keep a partial last line in a buffer until its newline arrives. In production, prefer a log shipper such as an agent that already handles this.

code.title: serialVersionUID mismatch

followUps:
Changes that break the stream's meaning are incompatible even with a fixed UID. Examples: changing a field's type (int to String), moving a class in the hierarchy, removing Serializable, or changing a class from serializable to Externalizable.

Compatible changes are adding fields (they get default values on old data), removing fields (the data is ignored), adding methods, and adding classes to the hierarchy. A fixed UID only stops the automatic check; it does not make unsafe changes safe, so you must judge each change.

Not in practice: for records, serialVersionUID is fixed at 0L by default and its value is not compared, so mismatches are never reported.

Records are serialized only by their components via the canonical constructor, so adding or reordering fields is handled by component names, and the usual UID matching is not used. You may declare one but it is ignored. Record serialization also avoids calling readObject, which makes it safer.

Technically yes, since Throwable implements Serializable, so a custom exception without a declared UID triggers the compiler lint warning -Xlint:serial.

Exceptions are serialized when they cross a JVM boundary, for example with RMI or when stored in a distributed cache. Declare private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;. Also make sure each field you add is serializable, or mark it transient.

code.title: transient fields and readObject

followUps:
readResolve() lets a class replace the object that was just deserialized with another one, usually to keep a singleton or an enum-like constant unique.

private Object readResolve() {
  return INSTANCE; // discard the new copy
}

Without it, deserializing a singleton creates a second instance and breaks the guarantee. It is also used by the serialization proxy pattern to return the real object. Enums need none, because the JVM guarantees one instance per constant.

Externalizable hands you full control: you write writeExternal and readExternal yourself, deciding exactly what bytes are saved, instead of the JVM walking the fields.

It also requires a public no-argument constructor, which is called on read before readExternal. It can give a smaller, faster format, but you maintain it by hand, and it is just as unsafe with untrusted data. With Serializable the field walk is automatic and transient marks what to skip.

Because a logger belongs to the class, not to one object, and static fields are never serialized, so you avoid a non-serializable logger blocking serialization.

If you keep a logger as an instance field, you must make it transient (and recreate it after reading), otherwise you get NotSerializableException. With private static final Logger LOG = ... nothing is stored and every deserialized object shares the one logger.

code.title: ObjectInputFilter allow-list

followUps:
It lists the classes you allow and then rejects everything else. The pattern syntax uses ; to separate items, ! to reject, and a final !* to deny the rest.

com.myapp.dto.*;java.util.*;java.lang.*;!*
// also limits: maxdepth=5;maxrefs=1000;maxbytes=10000

Set it per stream with setObjectInputFilter or globally with -Djdk.serialFilter=.... Keep the list small, since every allowed library class is a possible gadget.

No. JSON libraries are safer by default, but they become dangerous when they allow the payload to name the Java class to create, which is called polymorphic typing.

Example: Jackson's default typing, or enableDefaultTyping(), with a field like "@class": "SomeGadget" lets an attacker pick any class on the classpath, and several CVEs came from this. Use fixed target types, avoid default typing, or restrict it with a PolymorphicTypeValidator allow-list of base types.

Records are deserialized by calling their canonical constructor with the component values, never by running a custom readObject, so an attacker cannot hook into object construction.

It also means your constructor's validation always runs, so invalid state (for example a negative amount) is rejected. This does not make deserialization of untrusted data safe, because the stream can still name other classes, so keep the filter and still prefer JSON or Protobuf into records.

code.title: Exceptions across threads, Future and CompletableFuture

followUps:
Catch the exception inside the task and log it with the full trace, or set a handler so nobody has to call get().

executor.execute(() -> {
  try { work(); }
  catch (Throwable t) { log.error("task failed", t); }
});
Thread.setDefaultUncaughtExceptionHandler((th, e) -> log.error(th.getName(), e));

For submit, attach future.whenComplete on a CompletableFuture, or override afterExecute in a ThreadPoolExecutor subclass to inspect the throwable. One central wrapper is better than remembering it in every task.

exceptionally(fn) returns a new CompletableFuture, and whatever value fn returns becomes its successful result; it runs only when the previous stage failed.

Example: supplyAsync(() -> 1/0).exceptionally(e -> -1).join() gives -1. If the earlier stage succeeded, fn is skipped and the value passes through. To change either outcome, use handle, which gets both the result and the exception.

Use StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure (preview), which cancels the other subtasks once one fails; with plain futures you must cancel them yourself.

for (Future<?> f : futures) f.cancel(true); // interrupts if running

With ExecutorService, call invokeAny or loop through the others and call cancel(true) when one fails. With CompletableFuture, cancel on one stage does not cancel the others automatically, so keep the list and cancel it yourself. The tasks must react to interruption for this to work.
